newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Broaddus - U.S. economy at crucial juncture.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Broaddus - U.S. economy at crucial juncture.

text.p: Richmond Federal Reserve President Alfred Broaddus said Tuesday that the U.S. economy and economic policy were at a "crucial juncture" after six years of expansion, but that the outlook was bright.
Broaddus told a group of business economists that recent inflation reports were "quite encouraging" and that the economy appeared to be moving in the right direction.
Broaddus said that recent inflation reports were "quite encouraging" and that the price picture so far in the current expansion has been "benign."
But he expressed concern about the current high level of U.S. economic activity and said he would welcome a report on third quarter growth that showed some slowing of growth.
He noted that many economists expect the third quarter report, which is to be released Wednesday, to show a significantly lower rate of Gross Domestic Product growth.

A lower level of growth would keep the expansion from becoming an unsustainable boom that could feed inflation, Broaddus said. He noted that employment has been growing above normal trends and in a range which historically has been associated with rising inflationary pressures.
Although there has been evidence of some upward pressure on wages, it has been modest and overall labor costs "have been very well behaved," Broaddus added.
But he cautioned that there was no reason to become complacent about inflation.
"I think there are some fairly special factors that have helped restrain wage and price pressures so far in this expansion," Broaddus said.

He cited corporate restructuring and downsizing, which has has created anxiety among workers and discouraged them from demanding too much from their employers. He said sluggish economic conditions among U.S. trading partners have restrained demand for U.S. exports, keeping a lid on prices.
He also cited inflows of foreign capital, mostly for stock purchases, which he said helped finance a substantial flow of imports without a deceleration of the dollar.
The Fed must and will be vigilant in the fight against inflation, Broaddus said. The central bank has made progress in combating inflation but still lacks complete credibility.
He made clear that he feels that the central bank should not be content with keeping consumer price inflation around current levels of about three percent.
"A monetary policy strategy that accepts three percent as an objective cannot ... be a credible longer-term anti-inflationary strategy," he said.
He argued that the central bank should aim to lower the annual rise in consumer price index to about two percent then hold it there.

"Trying to take action to gradually move the CPI rate of inflation down from three percent at least twoards two percent then holding it there for the long haul ... that's the way the Fed can keep employment high," he said.

As for the federal government, it needs to put its fiscal house in order so as to enhance America's long-term growth prospects, he said. He backed changing the tax code so that investors do not pay taxes on profits from the sale of land, shares and other investments that merely arise from inflation.
